content: 1. Peer-led education has been identified as a potentially effective harm reduction strategy for men who have sex with men (MSM) engaging in chemsex, as discussed by Bedi et al. in the International Journal of STD & AIDS (2020). 2. Bourne et al. explored the harm reduction needs of gay men involved in chemsex in South London, highlighting the importance of tailored interventions in the International Journal of Drug Policy (2015). 3. De Angelis et al. utilized an evidence synthesis approach to estimate the prevalence of hepatitis C in England and Wales, as published in Statistical Methods in Medical Research (2009). 4. Grebely and Dore examined the feasibility of eradicating hepatitis C virus infection among people who inject drugs, emphasizing the challenges and opportunities in Antiviral Research (2014). 5. Harm Reduction International released a briefing note in 2021 addressing chemsex and harm reduction strategies for gay men and other MSM, underscoring the need for targeted interventions. 6. Henry K. reported that chemsex among MSM is associated with an increased risk of HIV, hepatitis C, and bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs), emphasizing the public health implications. 7. Herrijgers et al. conducted a qualitative study in Belgium to assess harm reduction practices and needs in the context of chemsex, with findings published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2020). 8. Kennedy et al. developed the Evidence Project risk of bias tool to evaluate the rigor of both randomized and non-randomized intervention studies, as detailed in Systematic Reviews (2019). 9. Maxwell, Shahmanesh, and Gafos systematically reviewed the literature on chemsex behaviors among MSM, providing insights into patterns and risks in the International Journal of Drug Policy (2019). 10. McCall et al. addressed the significance of understanding chemsex and its implications for public health in the British Medical Journal (2015). 11. Nelson et al. conducted systematic reviews on the global epidemiology of hepatitis B and C among people who inject drugs, presenting their findings in The Lancet (2011). 12. Newland and Kelly-Hanku performed a qualitative scoping review of sexualized drug use, including chemsex, among MSM and transgender women in Asia, published by APCOM in 2021. 13. Pakianathan et al. investigated the association between chemsex and new HIV diagnoses among MSM attending sexual health clinics, with results published in HIV Medicine (2018). 14. Sterne et al. introduced the ROBINS-I tool for assessing bias in non-randomized studies of interventions, as described in the British Medical Journal (2016). 15. Scheibe et al. reported on the prevalence of hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV, as well as related sexual and substance use risk practices among key populations in South Africa, in BMC Infectious Diseases (2020). 16. Sterne et al. revised the RoB 2 tool for evaluating bias in randomized trials, as detailed in the British Medical Journal (2019). 17. Tan et al. conducted a qualitative study on chemsex among MSM in Singapore, identifying challenges and potential interventions, as published in the International Journal of Drug Policy (2018). 18. Tomkins et al. systematically reviewed sexualized drug use among MSM, emphasizing the need for harm reduction strategies, as published in Perspectives in Public Health (2019). 19. Tomkins, Vivancos, and Ward conducted an online survey in Greater Manchester to identify the best ways to support individuals engaging in chemsex, with findings published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS (2018). 20. UNAIDS released the Global AIDS Update in 2021, focusing on lessons learned from 40 years of AIDS and their relevance to pandemic responses. 21. The UNAIDS/WHO Working Group on Global HIV/AIDS and STI Surveillance published strategies and laboratory methods for strengthening STI surveillance in 2012. 22. The World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidelines in 2021 for managing symptomatic sexually transmitted infections, emphasizing evidence-based approaches. 23. Williams et al. analyzed the incidence and transmission patterns of acute hepatitis C in the United States from 1982 to 2006, as published in the Archives of Internal Medicine (2011). 24. Wirtz et al. reviewed the epidemiology of HIV and viral hepatitis among imprisoned key populations, highlighting the need for targeted interventions in Epidemiologic Reviews (2018). 25. The WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations include systematic review findings and GRADE tables to inform evidence-based practices. 26. Yeh and Kennedy systematically reviewed the effectiveness of online interventions for HIV, viral hepatitis, and STI prevention and care among key populations, providing evidence for WHO guidelines. 27. Online service delivery for HIV, viral hepatitis, and STI prevention and care has been shown to be as effective as face-to-face services in reaching new populations and improving linkage to care, particularly among MSM in the United States. 28. A cost study in Canada found that syphilis testing campaign advertisements on hookup platforms had the lowest cost-per-click ratio compared to traditional social media platforms. 29. Online services for HIV, viral hepatitis, and STIs are a feasible and acceptable approach to expanding access to care for key populations, but further research is needed in low-resource settings and among populations other than MSM.
